name: Volcanic field
notes: Primary succession on lava, ash and cinder: nitrogen-fixing pioneer shrubs, tough grasses and mosses/lichens on bare rock, with ohia and birch/willow scrub where soil forms. Drawn on Hawaii (Kilauea/Mauna Loa), Iceland (Hekla, Surtsey), Mt St Helens, Etna and Mt Fuji.

growth.juvenile_note: Tiny two-winged nutlets sprout in early summer on moss, bare soil or burnt ground. Seedlings have minute round cotyledons, then small, downy, coarsely toothed, rounded leaves on hairy reddish twigs. At the treeline the young tree soon sprouts extra stems from its base, becoming a crooked, multi-stemmed bush with dark reddish-brown bark that whitens and peels only on older stems.

shrub.name: Green alder
shrub.origin: Mountains of Europe, Asia and N America

growth.juvenile_note: Tiny winged nutlets germinate on bare mineral ground, ash or pumice in the first wet spell. The seedling is a thin reddish stem with a few small, sticky, finely double-toothed oval leaves; root nodules fix nitrogen from the first year, so it grows on raw ash where little else can. Within a few years it sprouts more stems from the base and becomes a springy, many-stemmed clump whose stems curve downhill under the snow.
growth.source: Flora of North America (Alnus viridis subsp. sinuata/crispa: shrub to 3(-10) m, flowers with the leaves); Dale, Swanson & Crisafulli, Ecological Responses to the 1980 Eruption of Mount St. Helens (Sitka alder a chief woody colonist of the debris avalanche and mudflows); ages and rates estimated.

repro.note: nitrogen-fixing (Frankia root nodules): a pioneer of raw ash, pumice and scoria

shrub.source: Alnus alnobetula (Ehrh.) K.Koch (syn. Kew POWO (accepted name); Flora of North America; Flora of Japan.

shrub.name: Kukaenene

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds, dropped by nene and other birds, sprout in cracks of young pahoehoe and cinder. The seedling is a wiry reddish-brown stem with pairs of tiny, glossy, narrow dark leaves crowded along it; it soon branches and sprawls over the rock, rooting where stems touch, into a low dark-green mat studded with shiny black berries.
growth.source: Wagner, Herbst & Sohmer, Manual of the Flowering Plants of Hawai'i (prostrate or trailing shrub, leaves 5-12 mm, drupes black, glossy, on lava and cinder 1,000-3,000 m); rates and ages estimated.

ground.name: Map lichen

growth.juvenile_note: Begins as a thin black stain (prothallus) on bare, sunlit siliceous rock. Tiny angular chartreuse-yellow areoles (0.2-1.8 mm) appear on it like islands and multiply into a flat crust split by black lines, like a map; neighbouring thalli meet along black borders. Small black fruit bodies sit between the areoles. It widens by well under 1 mm a year.
growth.source: Wikipedia Rhizocarpon geographicum (patches to ~15 cm; areoles 0.2-1.8 mm; black apothecia under 1.5 mm; age estimates 9,500 yr on Baffin Island and 10,000-11,500 yr in the Brooks Range; used in lichenometry); diameter growth of roughly 0.1-1 mm/yr from lichenometry studies (knowledge)

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

epiphyte.name: Whisk fern

growth.juvenile_note: Spores germinate underground into a tiny (under 2 mm), colourless, branching gametophyte fed by mycorrhizal fungi. The young sporophyte pushes up a few thin, green, rootless stems that fork again and again into leafless 'whisks' with ribbed branches and tiny scale-like bumps, from a brown rhizome in rock cracks, tree-fern trunks or palm leaf bases; yellow, 3-lobed spore cases follow.
growth.source: Wikipedia Psilotum and P. nudum (subterranean mycoheterotrophic gametophyte under 2 mm; sporophyte to 30 cm or more, leafless, with a rootless rhizome; three-lobed synangia with yellow-white spores; epiphytic in the tropics, in rock crevices in temperate areas). Timings and lifespan estimated.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

epiphyte.source: Tropics worldwide on trunks and rock; leafless green forks; the most primitive living land plant. Kew POWO.
